title: Local Moran’s I
text:
Global Moran’s I told us that lung cancer SIRs in Pennsylvania are spatially autocorrelated: similar values tend to sit next to each other. It did not tell us where. Today we break that single number into 67 pieces, one per county. Reading: Rogerson & Yamada Ch. 4.

title: Local Moran’s I
text:
2.1 One number per county
Center the SIRs, \(z_i = x_i - \bar x\). Global Moran’s I (row-standardized weights) is
\[
I = \frac{\sum_i z_i \sum_j w_{ij} z_j}{\sum_i z_i^2}.
\]
The numerator is a sum over counties. Pull out each county’s term and you get local Moran’s I (Anselin 1995):
\[
I_i = \frac{z_i}{m_2} \sum_j w_{ij} z_j, \qquad m_2 = \frac{\sum_i z_i^2}{n}.
\]
In words: (my deviation) × (my neighbours’ average deviation), scaled by the variance. Averaging the \(I_i\) gives back the global \(I\).

title: Local Moran’s I
text:
2.2 Computing it
localmoran_perm() returns \(I_i\), a \(p\)-value, and the quadrant for every county.


Code
set.seed(374)
lisa <- localmoran_perm(pa$SIR, lw, nsim = 999)

pa <- pa |>
  mutate(
    Ii    = lisa[, "Ii"],
    p_sim = lisa[, "Pr(z != E(Ii)) Sim"],                   # p-value
    quad  = as.character(attr(lisa, "quadr")$mean)          # quadrant
  )

title: Local Moran’s I
text:
3.1 Reading the map

High-High (hot spot): high SIR, surrounded by high SIRs.
Low-Low (cold spot): low SIR, surrounded by low SIRs.
High-Low / Low-High (spatial outliers): a county that breaks from its surroundings.

Two cautions. A coloured county is the core of a local pattern; its neighbours are part of it even when they stay grey. And look at \(E_i\) in the table: a county with few expected cases can produce an extreme SIR, and a “cluster” by chance. We return to how many counties we are testing at once next session.
